rv.q: There is real delicacy, too, in her mapping of Shideh’s damaged interior landscape. In her impressive final scenes, a new sort of self-exposure is required, nothing to do with headscarves but built of an emotional transparency between mother and daughter that leaves them forearmed for future battles.
This is a pacy, intense, and refreshingly unusual kind of thriller – one that reminds us that the scariest things in life aren’t the ones that go bump in the night.
Nadia Latif directs Carmen Nasr’s stage adaptation of writer-filmmaker Babak Anvari’s celebrated Middle-Eastern spine tingler UNDER THE SHADOW from 2016.
Anvari's near-perfect film would be almost impossible to do justice to on stage, but Shideh's conundrum remains the stuff of nightmares.
It can’t sustain the delicate balance it has created – but it is undoubtedly both original and enjoyable.
Under the Shadow is proof that the stage can be every bit as scary as the cinema.

cn.t: This Iranian war-set horror delivers effective jump scares and a fierce lead performance, though critics find the psychological unraveling less compelling on stage than in the original film.
